Medical Quiz.question: ১) Which one is belongs to Enterovirus group?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Hepatitis A virus (HAV) belongs to the Enterovirus group (family: Picornaviridae). It is a small, non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus transmitted mainly by the faeco-oral route.

Other options:

  • Hepatitis B virus (HBV) → Belongs to Hepadnaviridae family; DNA virus.

  • Hepatitis C virus (HCV) → Belongs to Flaviviridae family; RNA virus.

  • Hepatitis D virus (HDV) → Defective RNA virus (Deltavirus) that requires HBV for replication.

Exam pearl:
HAV → Enterovirus (Picornavirus family) → Faeco-oral transmission.

Medical Quiz.question: ২) Complications of acute viral hepatitis excludes..?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Chronic liver disease is not a usual complication of acute viral hepatitis. Most cases of acute viral hepatitis resolve completely, especially infections caused by HAV and HEV.

Recognized complications of acute viral hepatitis include:

  • Cholestatic hepatitis → prolonged jaundice due to impaired bile flow.

  • Relapsing hepatitis → recurrence of symptoms and liver enzyme elevation after initial recovery.

  • Cholestasis → may occur due to intrahepatic bile flow obstruction.

Chronic liver disease is mainly a complication of infections that can become chronic, such as:

  • Hepatitis B

  • Hepatitis C

  • Hepatitis D

Exam pearl:
Acute viral hepatitis complications → Cholestatic hepatitis, relapsing hepatitis, fulminant hepatitis.
Chronic liver disease → Mainly HBV, HCV, HDV (persistent infection).

Medical Quiz.question: ৩) Which one is the most common Causes of cirrhosis of liver in our country?
Medical Quiz.exp:
In Bangladesh and many developing countries, the most common cause of liver cirrhosis is chronic viral hepatitis, particularly:

  • Chronic Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection

  • Chronic Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection

Persistent viral infection causes chronic inflammation, hepatocyte injury, fibrosis, and eventually cirrhosis.

Other options:

  • Alcohol → A major cause of cirrhosis in many Western countries, but less common in Bangladesh.

  • Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) → Increasing worldwide due to obesity and metabolic syndrome, but not the leading cause in our country.

  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis → Rare cause of cirrhosis.

Exam pearl:
Most common cause of cirrhosis in Bangladesh → Chronic viral hepatitis (especially HBV).

Medical Quiz.question: ৪) Screening test for CLD excludes..?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Screening tests for chronic liver disease (CLD) aim to identify common causes of chronic liver injury. Important screening investigations include:

  • Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) → Screens for chronic Hepatitis B infection.

  • Hepatitis C antibody (Anti-HCV) → Screens for Hepatitis C infection.

  • Ferritin → Helps screen for haemochromatosis (iron overload disorder), a cause of CLD.

TIBC (Total Iron Binding Capacity) is not a primary screening test for CLD. It is mainly used in the evaluation of iron deficiency anaemia and iron metabolism disorders.

Exam pearl:
CLD screening → HBsAg, Anti-HCV, Ferritin (haemochromatosis), autoimmune markers, metabolic tests.
TIBC → Iron deficiency workup, not routine CLD screening.

Medical Quiz.question: ৫) Hand examination of CLD patient, you have to be looked which of the following points..?
Medical Quiz.exp:
In a patient with chronic liver disease (CLD), hand examination is important because several characteristic signs may be present:

  • Digital clubbing → Can occur in chronic liver disease, especially with conditions like primary biliary cholangitis and hepatopulmonary syndrome.

  • Dupuytren’s contracture → Associated with chronic liver disease, particularly alcoholic liver disease.

  • Palmar erythema → A classic sign of CLD due to hormonal changes (increased oestrogen effect and vascular changes).

Therefore, all of the listed findings should be assessed during hand examination of a CLD patient.

Exam pearl:
CLD hand signs → Palmar erythema + Dupuytren’s contracture + Clubbing + Leukonychia.

Medical Quiz.question: ৬) Which drug reduce renal blood flow and causes hepato-renal failure in a case of CLD?
Medical Quiz.exp:
NSAIDs (Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) can precipitate hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) in patients with chronic liver disease (especially cirrhosis) by reducing renal blood flow.

Mechanism:

  • NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX) → decrease renal prostaglandin synthesis.

  • Reduced prostaglandins cause renal vasoconstriction → decreased renal blood flow and GFR.

  • This can trigger hepatorenal failure in vulnerable CLD patients.

Other options:

  • ACE inhibitors → Can reduce renal perfusion by blocking angiotensin II, but are not the classic drug causing HRS in CLD.

  • Anxiolytics → May worsen hepatic encephalopathy due to CNS depression.

  • Narcotics → Can precipitate encephalopathy and respiratory depression, but do not primarily reduce renal blood flow.

Exam pearl:
Cirrhosis + NSAIDs → renal vasoconstriction → hepatorenal syndrome risk.

Medical Quiz.question: ৭) Normal portal venous pressure is..?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Normal portal venous pressure is approximately 5–10 mmHg. Clinically significant portal hypertension is defined when the portal pressure gradient (HVPG) exceeds 5 mmHg, and complications usually occur when it reaches ≥10–12 mmHg.

Option analysis:

  • 2–5 mmHg → Too low; may represent lower end but not the usual normal range.

  • <7 mmHg → Incorrect because normal portal pressure is generally higher (around 5–10 mmHg).

  • 10 mmHg → Within the upper normal/near threshold range.

  • >12 mmHg → Indicates clinically significant portal hypertension with risk of variceal bleeding.

Exam pearl:
Normal portal pressure → ~5–10 mmHg
Portal hypertension → >10 mmHg
Variceal bleeding risk → Portal pressure ≥12 mmHg.

Medical Quiz.question: ৮) Which drug isn't used for prevention of variceal bleeding in a case of CLD patient?
Medical Quiz.exp:
For prevention of variceal bleeding in chronic liver disease (CLD) with portal hypertension, the main drugs used are non-selective beta blockers (NSBBs):

  • Propranolol → Used for primary and secondary prevention of variceal bleeding by reducing portal venous pressure.

  • Carvedilol → Used as an alternative NSBB; it also has additional α1-blocking activity, causing greater reduction in portal pressure.

Terlipressin is not used for prevention of variceal bleeding. It is a vasopressin analogue used in the acute management of active variceal hemorrhage and hepatorenal syndrome.

Exam pearl:
Variceal bleeding prevention → Propranolol / Nadolol / Carvedilol.
Acute variceal bleed control → Terlipressin + endoscopic band ligation.

Medical Quiz.question: ৯) Liver may be tender in all of the following condition excludes..?
১০) Which of the following is not a hepatotropic virus?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Hepatotropic viruses are viruses that primarily infect the liver and cause hepatitis. The major hepatotropic viruses are:

  • HAV

  • HBV

  • HCV

  • HDV

  • HEV

Some non-hepatotropic viruses can also cause hepatitis as part of systemic infection, including:

  • CMV → can cause hepatitis, especially in immunocompromised patients.

  • EBV → can cause mild hepatitis during infectious mononucleosis.

  • HSV → can cause severe hepatitis (especially in neonates and immunocompromised patients).

HPV (Human papillomavirus) is not a hepatotropic virus and is associated mainly with skin and mucosal lesions and cervical cancer.

Exam pearl:
HPV → Papillomavirus → warts and cervical cancer; not hepatitis.

Medical Quiz.question: ১১) Routes of HBV infection through Vertical transmission is about..% cases?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Vertical transmission (mother-to-child transmission) of Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a major route of infection, especially in high endemic areas.

  • When a mother is HBsAg positive and HBeAg positive, the risk of transmission to the newborn is very high (around 90% without prophylaxis).

  • Most infections acquired through the perinatal route progress to chronic hepatitis B.

Other options:

  • 10% → Too low for high-risk vertical transmission.

  • 30% → Not the typical figure.

  • 70% → High but not the commonly quoted risk.

Exam pearl:
HBV vertical transmission risk ≈ 90% if mother is HBeAg positive.
Perinatal HBV infection → high risk of chronic carrier state.

Medical Quiz.question: ১২) Intramuscular injection of hyperimmune serum should be given within... Hours of accidental needle prick during operation of HBsAg(+ve) patient?
Medical Quiz.exp:
After an accidental needle prick exposure from an HBsAg-positive patient, Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) (hyperimmune serum) should be given as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours of exposure to provide passive immunity.

Management depends on the vaccination status of the exposed person:

  • Unvaccinated person → HBIG + start Hepatitis B vaccine series.

  • Previously vaccinated with adequate anti-HBs titre → No treatment usually required.

  • Vaccination status unknown/inadequate → HBIG and vaccination as indicated.

Other options:

  • 6 hours, 12 hours → Too early and not the standard exam answer.

  • 36 hours → Beyond the recommended optimal window.

Exam pearl:
HBV needle-stick exposure → HBIG + vaccine, ideally within 24 hours.

Medical Quiz.question: ১৩) Full recovery occurs in .... % of adults following acute HBV infection?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Following acute Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in adults, the majority of patients achieve complete recovery, with approximately 95–98% clearing the infection spontaneously.

  • Adults have a strong immune response against HBV, leading to:

    • Clearance of HBsAg

    • Development of anti-HBs antibodies

    • Lifelong immunity in most cases

A small proportion of adults (around 2–5%) fail to clear the virus and progress to chronic hepatitis B infection.

Other options:

  • 80–85% → Too low for adults.

  • 85–90% → Underestimates recovery rate.

  • 90–95% → Close but lower than the commonly accepted figure.

Exam pearl:
Acute HBV infection in adults → 95–98% recover; 2–5% become chronic carriers.

Medical Quiz.question: ১৪) All of the followings are the complication of liver abscess excludes..?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Liver abscess can cause complications due to local extension or blood-borne spread. Common complications include:

  • Pleural effusion → Can occur, especially with a right lobe liver abscess due to diaphragmatic irritation or rupture into the pleural space.

  • Pericardial effusion → Rare but possible, especially with left lobe liver abscess extending toward the pericardium.

  • Septicaemia → Occurs due to spread of infection into the bloodstream.

Haematogenous spread to GIT is not a typical complication of liver abscess. Spread is usually through the portal circulation, systemic circulation, or direct extension, not from liver abscess to GIT via blood.

Exam pearl:
Liver abscess complications → Rupture into pleura/pericardium, septicaemia, and metastatic infection (especially brain/lung).

Medical Quiz.question: ১৫) Which type of fever occurs in liver abscess?
Medical Quiz.exp:
The typical fever pattern seen in liver abscess is intermittent fever. It occurs due to periodic release of inflammatory mediators and may be associated with rigors and chills, especially in pyogenic liver abscess.

Other options:

  • Continued fever → Temperature remains persistently elevated with minimal fluctuation; seen in conditions like lobar pneumonia and typhoid (classically).

  • Remittent fever → Temperature fluctuates but does not return to normal; seen in some infections.

  • Quotidian fever → Fever occurring once daily at regular intervals; classically associated with malaria patterns and some inflammatory disorders.

Exam pearl:
Liver abscess → Intermittent fever + chills/rigors + tender hepatomegaly.

Medical Quiz.question: ১৬) Which organism is responsible for amoebic liver abscess?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Amoebic liver abscess (ALA) is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, an intestinal protozoan parasite.

Mechanism:

  • The parasite infects the colon and penetrates the intestinal mucosa.

  • It reaches the liver through the portal vein.

  • It causes hepatic necrosis and abscess formation, classically producing “anchovy sauce” pus.

Other options:

  • Echinococcus granulosus → Causes hydatid (echinococcal) cyst of the liver.

  • Ancylostoma duodenale → Hookworm causing iron deficiency anaemia.

  • Bacteroides → Anaerobic bacteria associated with pyogenic liver abscess, not amoebic abscess.

Exam pearl:
Amoebic liver abscess → Entamoeba histolytica → Portal spread from colon → Anchovy sauce pus.

Medical Quiz.question: ১৭) Which anti TB drug isn't responsible for hepatitis?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Amoebic liver abscess (ALA) is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, an intestinal protozoan parasite.

Mechanism:

  • The parasite infects the colon and penetrates the intestinal mucosa.

  • It reaches the liver through the portal vein.

  • It causes hepatic necrosis and abscess formation, classically producing “anchovy sauce” pus.

Other options:

  • Echinococcus granulosus → Causes hydatid (echinococcal) cyst of the liver.

  • Ancylostoma duodenale → Hookworm causing iron deficiency anaemia.

  • Bacteroides → Anaerobic bacteria associated with pyogenic liver abscess, not amoebic abscess.

Exam pearl:
Amoebic liver abscess → Entamoeba histolytica → Portal spread from colon → Anchovy sauce pus.

Medical Quiz.question: ১৮) Which one is the features of decompensated CLD?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Decompensated chronic liver disease (CLD) occurs when the cirrhotic liver fails to maintain normal function. The major features of decompensation are:

  • Jaundice → Due to impaired bilirubin metabolism and excretion.

  • Ascites

  • Variceal bleeding

  • Hepatic encephalopathy

Other options:

  • Fever → Suggests infection (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) but is not a defining feature of CLD decompensation.

  • Leukonychia → A chronic liver disease sign (e.g., Terry’s nails), but not a feature of decompensation.

  • Palmar erythema → A stigmata of chronic liver disease due to hormonal changes, but not a marker of decompensation.

Exam pearl:
Decompensated CLD = Jaundice + Ascites + Variceal bleeding + Hepatic encephalopathy.

Medical Quiz.question: ১৯) Serum level of HBsAg may be rise in which of the following condition?
Medical Quiz.exp:
Serum HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) levels may be increased in leprosy due to the association between Hepatitis B infection and leprosy, particularly in endemic areas. Some studies have shown a higher prevalence of HBsAg positivity among leprosy patients.

Other options:

  • TB → Not associated with increased serum HBsAg levels.

  • Malignant melanoma → No typical association with HBsAg elevation.

  • Liver abscess → May affect liver function but does not cause increased HBsAg levels.

Exam pearl:
HBsAg positivity can be seen more frequently in leprosy patients.
HBsAg = marker of current HBV infection (acute or chronic).

Medical Quiz.question: ২০) Which statement is most suitable regarding liver abscess?
Medical Quiz.option1: Pyogenic liver abscess is more common
Medical Quiz.option3: Amoebic liver abscess shows single lesion
Medical Quiz.option4: Prognosis is better in pyogenic than amoebic
Medical Quiz.exp:
Pyogenic liver abscess (PLA) is now considered the more common type of liver abscess compared with amoebic liver abscess in many regions, especially due to bacterial infections and hepatobiliary disease.

Other options:

  • CBC shows eosinophilia in pyogenic → Incorrect. Eosinophilia is more suggestive of parasitic infections (e.g., hydatid disease), not pyogenic abscess.

  • Amoebic liver abscess shows single lesion → Generally true (usually solitary right lobe lesion), but it is not the most suitable statement compared with the epidemiological fact that pyogenic abscess is more common.

  • Prognosis is better in pyogenic than amoebic → Incorrect. Amoebic liver abscess usually has a better prognosis with appropriate treatment; pyogenic abscess may have higher mortality, especially in elderly or septic patients.

Exam pearl:
Liver abscess types → Pyogenic (bacterial) is more common; Amoebic abscess → Entamoeba histolytica, usually solitary right lobe lesion with anchovy sauce pus.
